Abstract Objectives: This study aims to explore the representations of hybrid identity among the children Received: 18/9/2024 of mixed Saudi families, the factors contributing to its emergence, and the extent to which it Revised: 28/9/2024 facilitates integration or assimilation into Saudi society. Accepted: 8/10/2024 Published online: 1/10/2025 Methods: The research followed a case study approach, with data collected through a snowball sampling technique. Semi-structured remote interviews were employed as the data collection tool. The study included seven participants from mixed Saudi families. * Corresponding author: Results: The study yielded several key findings. First, participants exhibited three forms of maldraiwish@ksu.edu.sa identity: fused hybrid identity, alternating identity, and unidirectional identity. Second, factors such as birthplace, upbringing, strong familial ties between the mother's family and the children, Citation: Alduraywish, M. A. (2025). and geographical proximity to the mother were significant in shaping hybrid identity. JSON: Name: saudi_mixed_hybrid_identity Title: A sequential mixed-methods study using qualitative case study and quantitative survey to identify determinants of hybrid identity orientation among children of Saudi mixed families Short Hypothesis: Greater maternal-family proximity during childhood (measured by years of co-residence and frequency of caregiving contact) increases the probability that a child of a Saudi mixed family will adopt a fused hybrid identity orientation rather than an alternating or unidirectional identity orientation. Related Work: Prior research on cross‐national and mixed‐family identity combines two broad approaches: large‐scale demographic analyses of intermarriage trends (population/census studies) and small‐sample qualitative studies of bicultural/hybrid identity formation. Demographic approaches quantify marriage patterns and correlations with socioeconomic variables, but they lack individual‐level psychological and relational measures and cannot describe identity phenomenology. Qualitative studies (third‐space, hybridity, bicultural orientation frameworks) provide rich typologies and subjective accounts but are often limited to Western contexts, use small convenience samples, and rarely operationalize identity types for statistical testing. Work on bicultural identity orientation develops psychometric scales but has focused on immigrant contexts and not on mixed‐family offspring in conservative national contexts; it also commonly treats identity as dichotomous (bicultural vs monocultural) rather than multi‐modal (fused/alternating/unidirectional). Across approaches there is a gap: limited causal testing linking precise family/geographic predictors (birthplace, co‐residence, maternal kin ties, proximity) to empirically validated identity typologies in under‐studied national contexts such as Saudi Arabia, and limited mixed‐method pipelines that convert qualitative typologies into testable quantitative instruments. Abstract: This study addresses how family and geographic factors shape hybrid identity orientations among children of Saudi mixed families. We propose a sequential mixed‐methods pipeline: (1) inductive qualitative case work to derive an empirically grounded typology of identity orientations and to generate measurement items; (2) construction of a standardized survey instrument; and (3) quantitative hypothesis testing of specific causal relationships between childhood maternal‐family proximity, birthplace/upbringing, social network ties, and identity orientation using multivariate statistical models. The main contribution is a validated, reproducible pipeline that translates rich interview‐based typologies (fused, alternating, unidirectional) into operational measures and then quantitatively tests predictor→identity relationships in a Saudi context. Expected outcomes are (a) a reproducible identity orientation scale calibrated to mixed‐family cases, (b) estimation of effect sizes for maternal proximity and related predictors, and (c) an evidence base informing social research and policy debates about cultural integration and family dynamics among mixed families in Saudi Arabia. Experiments: Dataset and recruitment: Phase 1 qualitative: purposive sample n=20 semi‐structured interviews (adults aged 18–40) drawn from Saudi mixed families (one Saudi parent + one non‐Saudi parent), balanced by gender and maternal region (GCC/non‐GCC/Asian/African/Western); interviews recorded, transcribed, translated as needed. Phase 2 quantitative: cross‐sectional survey n=360 target (power calculation for multinomial logistic regression with 10 predictors, power=0.8, alpha=0.05); recruitment via stratified snowball, university alumni, NGOs; inclusion criteria as above. Measures: dependent variable identity_orientation — categorical label (fused / alternating / unidirectional) and continuous identity_mix_score (1–7 Likert). Predictors: maternal_family_proximity (years co‐residence, frequency_of_contact per month), birthplace_binary (born_in_saudi), upbringing_duration_in_saudi (years before age 18), maternal_language_proficiency (self‐rated), crossborder_friend_index (count of close friends abroad), parental_education, household_SES, gender, age. Instrument construction: derive items from qualitative coding; compute Cronbach's alpha and confirmatory factor analysis for scale structure. Baselines: Baseline A: demographics only (age, gender, SES); Baseline B: demographics + birthplace/upbringing; Target Model C: demographics + family_proximity + social_networks + language. Statistical analyses: primary test — multinomial logistic regression predicting identity_orientation; report odds ratios, 95% CI, p‐values, and marginal effects. Model comparison metrics: AIC, BIC, likelihood ratio tests, McFadden pseudo‐R^2. Robustness: propensity score matching on birthplace/upbringing to reduce confounding; sensitivity analysis varying identity labeling threshold; alternative models: ordinal logistic (for identity_mix_score) and random forest classifier for predictive accuracy. Cross‐validation: 5‐fold CV for predictive models, report mean accuracy, F1 per class. Ablation studies: (1) remove maternal_family_proximity from Model C and report ΔAIC/Δpseudo‐R^2; (2) remove crossborder_friend_index; (3) test interviewer_mode effect (remote vs in‐person) by including mode dummy and interaction terms. Qualitative validation: inter‐coder reliability (Cohen's kappa ≥ 0.70) on thematic codes; triangulate interview typology labels with self‐reported survey identity items. Significance thresholds: two‐tailed p<0.05. Software: R or Python for statistical modelling; NVivo or similar for qualitative coding. Risk Factors and Limitations: Sampling bias: reliance on snowball and online recruitment will oversample socially networked or urban respondents and underrepresent rural, undocumented, or politically sensitive cases. Social desirability and reporting bias: identity and family topics are sensitive; participants may misreport upbringing, maternal ties, or identity orientation. Measurement error: operationalizing complex identity types into discrete categories risks reductionism and misclassification; translation and cross‐language scale equivalence can introduce noise. Confounding and causal identification: observational data limit causal claims; residual confounding (e.g., parental attitudes, legal status, schooling quality) may bias estimates. Small cell sizes: some identity categories or maternal origin strata may be rare, reducing statistical power and inflating variance of estimates. Generalization limits: findings will be specific to Saudi sociocultural, legal, and historical context and may not transfer to other national settings. Mode effects and remote interviewing: remote interviews may reduce rapport and depth compared with in‐person interviews, affecting typology generation. Ethical and legal sensitivity: discussing mixed marriages and identity may expose participants to social risk; legal/administrative constraints could limit recruitment. Computational limits: none major for analyses envisaged, but extensive qualitative coding is time‐intensive and requires trained coders.
